## PLAINS - Birth is supported by experienced women; anchor communities or slower groups provide stability when needed. - Infants are carried while adults work and learn through constant observation.

- Infants are carried while adults work and learn through constant observation. - Children gradually copy useful adult tasks; aptitude is observed, but community need can override preference. - Adulthood is demonstrated by reliable contribution to survival.
## MOUNTAINS - Birth occurs within the extended specialist lineage. - Infants remain immersed in their specialist family's environment.

## Geographic foundation The Great Plains are Hearth's largest human landscape, within the continent's ~1.5 million people. The Hearth population layer allocates 450,000 people (30%) to grassland/woodland environments. Residential communities generally run ~80–150 people, with smaller groups and larger seasonal aggregations possible. Hearth has strong connectivity and gene flow.
## Anchor communities Semi-permanent/repeatedly used locations support: - elders who can no longer travel;
Household sleeping/family arrangements do not determine daytime work-group membership.
Night-oriented activity is especially hunter-heavy, with scouts and lookouts supporting it.

**Purpose:** Living world reference and canon ledger.

- Two moons: one larger/farther, one smaller/closer, visually similar in apparent size. - Two moons contribute secondary tidal/geological effects but do **not** directly push continents; internal planetary heat and mantle dynamics remain the fundamental tectonic driver. - Sky may have a subtle greenish cast; exact atmospheric chemistry remains open.

- Civilization is constrained less by what humans can understand than by what they can safely sustain. - Human settlements are preferentially established where environments are **dramatically safer than surrounding alternatives**, not because any location is truly safe. - Humans learn migration patterns, terrain, animal behavior, weather, resources, and other environmental information because knowledge equals survival.
## Four major continental systems

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

### Seasonal high-ground gatherings Three or four villages may occupy a broad territory, for example within ~25 km of one another. During major wet-season/monsoon flooding they can converge on one shared high-ground location, temporarily bringing together roughly **250–500 people**.

### Density distinction Great Plains communities can be somewhat larger, potentially up to ~200 people, because broad meat, grain/seed, and plant abundance can support greater concentration. Wetland communities remain ~80–120 but periodically form much larger gatherings when environmental conditions force them onto shared high ground.

### Still to develop Family/household organization; partnerships; kinship; reproduction; lineage; leadership; dispute resolution; death; beliefs; material culture; arts; trade; inter-community politics.

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

- Two moons: one larger/farther, one smaller/closer, visually similar in apparent size. - Two moons contribute secondary tidal/geological effects but do **not** directly push continents; internal planetary heat and mantle dynamics remain the fundamental tectonic driver. - Sky may have a subtle greenish cast; exact atmospheric chemistry remains open.

- Civilization is constrained less by what humans can understand than by what they can safely sustain. - Human settlements are preferentially established where environments are **dramatically safer than surrounding alternatives**, not because any location is truly safe. - Humans learn migration patterns, terrain, animal behavior, weather, resources, and other environmental information because knowledge equals survival.
## Four major continental systems

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

### Seasonal high-ground gatherings Three or four villages may occupy a broad territory, for example within ~25 km of one another. During major wet-season/monsoon flooding they can converge on one shared high-ground location, temporarily bringing together roughly **250–500 people**.

### Density distinction Great Plains communities can be somewhat larger, potentially up to ~200 people, because broad meat, grain/seed, and plant abundance can support greater concentration. Wetland communities remain ~80–120 but periodically form much larger gatherings when environmental conditions force them onto shared high ground.

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

### Seasonal high-ground gatherings Three or four villages may occupy a broad territory, for example within ~25 km of one another. During major wet-season/monsoon flooding they can converge on one shared high-ground location, temporarily bringing together roughly **250–500 people**.

### Density distinction Great Plains communities can be somewhat larger, potentially up to ~200 people, because broad meat, grain/seed, and plant abundance can support greater concentration. Wetland communities remain ~80–120 but periodically form much larger gatherings when environmental conditions force them onto shared high ground.

## Social unit The extended specialist household/lineage is the core unit.

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

### Seasonal high-ground gatherings Three or four villages may occupy a broad territory, for example within ~25 km of one another. During major wet-season/monsoon flooding they can converge on one shared high-ground location, temporarily bringing together roughly **250–500 people**.

### Density distinction Great Plains communities can be somewhat larger, potentially up to ~200 people, because broad meat, grain/seed, and plant abundance can support greater concentration. Wetland communities remain ~80–120 but periodically form much larger gatherings when environmental conditions force them onto shared high ground.

## 1. Continental Identity

Hearth is a mostly intact great continental landmass. Its defining geographic character is continuity: enormous interior distances, broad connected watersheds, old continental terrain, and mountain systems concentrated toward portions of its active margins.
**Canonical status:** Foundational working World reference / current consolidation checkpoint   **Purpose:** Living canon ledger for the prehistoric/anachronistic world currently being created.

- Animals should not exist merely as decorative monsters or spectacle. - The world is intended to support stories rather than function as an exhaustive encyclopedia. - The world's biological identity should feel **prehistoric before it feels alien**.
The moons do **not** simply push continents around.
Planetary interior dynamics and plate tectonics remain the fundamental drivers of continental movement.

### Communities Normal communities: **~80–120 people**. They favor elevated ground, natural islands, ridges, stable banks, and other reliable locations. A community thinks of its territory as a network of usable places rather than one permanent settlement.

### Seasonal high-ground gatherings Three or four villages may occupy a broad territory, for example within ~25 km of one another. During major wet-season/monsoon flooding they can converge on one shared high-ground location, temporarily bringing together roughly **250–500 people**.

### Density distinction Great Plains communities can be somewhat larger, potentially up to ~200 people, because broad meat, grain/seed, and plant abundance can support greater concentration. Wetland communities remain ~80–120 but periodically form much larger gatherings when environmental conditions force them onto shared high ground.

### Still to develop Family/household organization; partnerships; kinship; reproduction; lineage; leadership; dispute resolution; death; beliefs; material culture; arts; trade; inter-community politics.

Repeated-use anchor communities support elders who cannot travel, very young children, injured/recovering people, storage, crafts, teaching, animal management and recurring social life. 4. Practical travel groups generally contain ~10–25 people, with ~10–15 a common small unit.

7. Peaceful outsiders are generally welcomed; hospitality is reciprocal survival infrastructure, not automatic trust. 8. Households, work/travel groups, communities and the wider Plains network are distinct layers of belonging. 9. Children learn through observation, play, useful participation and need-driven training.

11. Skills are redundantly distributed so critical knowledge does not depend on one individual. 12. Leadership is functional and situational; authority comes from demonstrated competence and trust in a specific responsibility. 13. Serious mistakes are distinguished from negligence/recklessness; accountability focuses on whether trust remains.

5. When the community fishes, most able-bodied members participate. 6. Elders, very young children, injured people, caregivers, watchkeepers, and task-excluded people remain in necessary supporting roles. 7. After major work, the community commonly reconvenes for communal meals.

11. Coastal peoples develop deliberate small-scale salt collection/evaporation and use salt for preservation, especially fish. 12. Salt-based preservation increases food security and can support somewhat larger/stabler communities where ecology permits. 13. The Coastal peoples remain exposed to severe marine and weather hazards; preservation and versatility are resilience mechanisms, not guarantees of safety.
